question: A 70-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination of diffuse exertional chest pain which he has successfully been treating with sublingual nitroglycerin for the past year. The patient has been taking lisinopril daily for essential hypertension. His pulse is 75/min and regular, and blood pressure is 155/90 mm Hg. Cardiac and pulmonary examination show no abnormalities; there is no peripheral edema. A decrease of which of the following is the most likely explanation for the improvement of this patient's chest pain?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Sublingual nitroglycerin" -> "vasodilation of coronary arteries" -> "increased blood flow to myocardium" -> "reduction in myocardial oxygen demand" -> "improvement of exertional chest pain" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Lisinopril" -> "decreased peripheral arterial resistance" -> "lowered afterload" -> "improved ventricular function" -> "reduction in exertional chest pain" -> 80%
CHAIN: "Decreased venous return" -> "reduced preload" -> "lowered end-diastolic pressure" -> "decreased myocardial wall stress" -> "improvement in chest pain" -> 75%
CHAIN: "Decreased end-diastolic pressure" -> "reduced myocardial oxygen demand" -> "improved perfusion during exertion" -> "less chest pain during activity" -> 90%
CHAIN: "Improved ventricular compliance" -> "better filling during diastole" -> "increased stroke volume" -> "reduction in exertional chest pain" -> 70%
analysis: The patient has been using sublingual nitroglycerin, which is a vasodilator. Nitroglycerin primarily decreases preload by causing venous dilation, leading to venous pooling and a reduction in end-diastolic pressure. This reduction in preload can improve symptoms of angina by decreasing the workload on the heart and improving myocardial oxygen supply-demand balance. Therefore, the most likely explanation for the improvement of this patient's chest pain is a decrease in end-diastolic pressure.
